title: Standing Up
objectives: I can explain what courage, loyalty, and fairness look like using ten words.
I can use context clues to understand words about people who resist unfair rules.
I can tell the difference between defying a rule and working to change it.
I can write about an injustice and a campaign to fix it.
rationale: Standing Up gives fifth graders the vocabulary of civil courage, which they meet in social studies and in biography. The ten words move from the act (defy, vow, campaign) to the person (valiant, noble, rebel) to the values behind the action (dignity, conviction, devotion, injustice). Several words carry a second sense (conviction, noble, campaign) so students learn to check meaning in context. The unit reuses assertive and daring from earlier units and debate from unit 2, so the vocabulary of speaking up builds across the year.

words.def: To refuse openly to obey or accept something.
words.ex: In 1955, Rosa Parks defied a segregation law by refusing to give up her bus seat.
words.ex2: The sailors decided to defy the captain's order and turn back, because they knew the storm was too dangerous.
words.nonExample: Following the safety rules at the pool is not defying them.

apps.academic: In history, many groups defied laws they believed were unfair.
apps.spoken: I will not defy my coach, but I will ask a question.
apps.writing: Use defy for an open refusal, often one that takes courage.

cloze.s: The villagers chose to ___ the king's order and kept the old market open, even though soldiers stood at the gate.

cloze2.s: The class decided to ___ the unfair rule by wearing the same color together and asking the principal to change it.

misuse.s: The students defy the teacher by following every direction exactly and politely.

words.def: Showing great courage when facing danger or difficulty.
words.ex: The valiant firefighter went back into the smoky building to check for anyone left inside.
words.ex2: Despite her fear, Mia made a valiant effort to finish the race.
words.nonExample: Running away at the first sign of trouble is not valiant.

apps.academic: Old stories often praise a valiant knight or a brave explorer.
apps.spoken: That was a valiant try, even though we lost.
apps.writing: Use valiant for courage shown against real difficulty, even if the person does not win.

words.def: The quality of deserving respect; calm pride in yourself.
words.ex: The coach treated every player with dignity, even the ones who lost the game.
words.ex2: She walked out of the room with dignity after her mistake and stood tall.
words.nonExample: Teasing someone in front of a crowd does not respect their dignity.

apps.academic: Many human rights documents say that every person has dignity.
apps.spoken: Everyone deserves to be treated with dignity.
apps.writing: Use dignity for the respect a person deserves and the calm pride they show.

cloze.s: Even when the crowd was jeering, the young skater held her head high and finished her routine with ___.

cloze2.s: The new rule said each worker must be treated with ___ and given a fair chance to speak.

misuse.s: The winner's dignity grew when she laughed at the other players' mistakes.
misuse.why: Dignity comes from respect for yourself and others, not from laughing at them.

visual.alt: A person standing tall under a bright star.

words.def: A strong belief that you hold firmly.

senses.def: a court's decision that a person is guilty of a crime
senses.example: The judge announced the conviction after the jury finished its vote.

words.ex: She spoke with conviction because she truly believed the river must be cleaned.
words.ex2: His conviction that all children deserve books led him to start a free library.
words.nonExample: A guess you would drop at the first question is not a conviction.

apps.academic: A speech with conviction shows that the speaker believes it is true and important.
apps.writing: Use conviction for a deep belief that guides what someone does.

cloze.s: Although many people laughed at her idea, Alma spoke with great ___ because she was sure it was right.

cloze2.s: His ___ that all people should be treated fairly led him to join the march.

misuse.s: His conviction was so weak that he changed his mind every time someone sneezed.
misuse.why: A conviction is a strong belief held firmly; changing your mind at every small thing is the opposite.

visual.alt: A thought bubble glowing with flames.

words.def: Strong love and loyalty toward a person, cause, or activity.
words.ex: Her devotion to the team showed when she practiced every morning before school.
words.ex2: The nurse's devotion to her patients kept her at the hospital long after her shift ended.
words.nonExample: Quitting the first time something gets hard is not devotion.

apps.academic: Biographies often describe a person's devotion to a cause.
apps.spoken: Her devotion to her little brother is clear.
apps.writing: Use devotion to show loyalty that lasts through hard times.

cloze.s: The dog's ___ to its owner was obvious: it waited at the gate every afternoon, rain or shine.

cloze2.s: Years of ___ to the project, including weekends and late nights, finally paid off when the library opened.

misuse.s: Her devotion to the club was clear because she never came to meetings and never helped.
misuse.why: Devotion means strong loyalty; never helping shows no loyalty.

words.def: Having high moral qualities such as honesty and courage.

senses.def: a person born into a high rank in society
senses.example: The nobles gathered in the castle to hear the king's plan.

words.ex: It was a noble act to return the lost wallet without taking a single dollar.
words.ex2: The noble king shared his food with the hungry travelers.
words.nonExample: Taking credit for someone else's work is not noble.

apps.academic: In history, a noble goal such as freedom can inspire many people.
apps.spoken: That was a noble thing to do.
apps.writing: Use noble for actions or goals that show high character, not only for rank.

cloze.s: Giving up her seat on the crowded bus so an older man could sit down was a ___ gesture.

cloze2.s: The group had a ___ goal: to clean the river so that every family could fish safely.

misuse.why: Noble means showing high moral character; lying and keeping money is not noble.

words.frame: A noble thing to do is ___.

words.def: A person who fights against the people in charge.
words.ex: The rebel leader urged everyone to stand against the unfair taxes.
words.ex2: The little sister was a rebel who refused to wear the shoes her parents picked.
words.nonExample: A student who follows every rule of the class is not a rebel.

apps.academic: Some rebels in history fought for freedom, and others fought for power.
apps.spoken: You wore two different socks on purpose? What a rebel!
apps.writing: Use rebel for someone who resists those in charge, and judge whether the cause is fair.

cloze.s: The ___ crossed the border at night and urged the villagers to stand against the harsh ruler.

cloze2.s: Nobody expected the quiet student to become a ___, but she led the protest against wasting cafeteria food.

misuse.s: The rebel obeyed every order and never questioned the rulers.
misuse.why: A rebel resists those in charge; obeying every order is the opposite.

words.def: A situation or act that is not fair or right.
words.ex: Students saw an injustice when only some of them were punished for the same mistake.
words.ex2: Many people marched to protest the injustice of unequal pay.
words.nonExample: A fair rule that applies to everyone is not an injustice.

apps.academic: Biographies often show how one person worked to end an injustice.
apps.spoken: It feels like an injustice that only one team got a turn.
apps.writing: Use injustice for unfair treatment, especially when it affects many people.

cloze.s: Giving the prize to the player who cheated was an ___ that made the whole team angry.

cloze2.s: The article described the ___ of a rule that let only some children attend the town's best school.

misuse.s: It was an injustice when everyone received the same fair treatment and a fair turn.
misuse.why: An injustice is something unfair; fair treatment for everyone is not an injustice.

words.def: To make a serious promise to do something.
words.ex: The explorers vowed to return and finish the map.
words.ex2: At the ceremony, the new citizens vowed to respect the laws of their country.
words.nonExample: A quick "maybe I will" is not a vow.

apps.academic: Characters in myths often vow to finish a hard task.
apps.spoken: I vow to keep your secret.
apps.writing: Use vow for a promise made seriously, often with strong feeling.

cloze.s: After the flood, the neighbors ___ to rebuild every house on the street before winter.

cloze2.s: Standing before the class, Eli will ___ to treat every classmate with respect, and the teacher wrote his promise on the board.

misuse.s: I vow that my bike is red.
misuse.why: A vow is a serious promise about what you will do, not a statement of a fact.

visual.alt: A raised hand beside a written promise.

words.def: A planned series of actions to reach a goal, such as winning an election.

senses.def: to work in an organized way for a goal
senses.example: She campaigned for a new crosswalk outside the school.

words.ex: The class started a campaign to collect books for the new library.
words.ex2: Her campaign for class president included posters, speeches, and a plan for a garden.
words.nonExample: One quick comment in the hallway is not a campaign.

apps.academic: A historian may study a military campaign or a campaign for voting rights.
apps.spoken: We started a campaign to save the old park.
apps.writing: Use campaign for an organized effort that lasts over time.

cloze.s: The students launched a ___ to raise money for the animal shelter, with posters, a bake sale, and a collection box at every door.

cloze2.s: Months of speeches and posters made up her ___ for class president, and she won by ten votes.

misuse.s: A campaign is a single quiet wish that nobody ever plans or shares.
misuse.why: A campaign is an organized effort over time; a quiet wish is not.

passage.title: Save the Library
paras: When the town council announced that it would close the library, Ana felt it was an injustice. The library had been her second home since she was five. Her devotion to its shelves was well known, and she had read every book in the animal section twice.

At school, she and her friends began a campaign to save the library. They made posters and collected signatures. Theo wanted to defy the council by sleeping inside the building. "That makes us rebels," he said proudly. Ana disagreed. "Breaking rules would give them a reason to ignore us," she said. She spoke with conviction, and her friends listened.

On the night of the council meeting, three hundred people filled the hall. Ana's hands shook, but she stood at the microphone and read the signatures. "A library is a place where every person is treated with dignity," she said, "even people who cannot afford to buy a single book." Some adults called it a noble speech. One man whispered that it was valiant for a ten-year-old to speak before so many people.
After a long silence, the council voted to keep the doors open. That night Ana made a vow: she would volunteer at the library every Saturday.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "defy" means to
qs.why: Theo wants to sleep in the building against the council's order, so defy means to openly refuse to obey.

qs.q: Why does Ana disagree with Theo's plan to sleep inside the library?
choices: She is afraid of the dark.
She thinks breaking rules would give the council a reason to ignore them.
She wants to read more books.
qs.why: Ana says that breaking rules would give the council a reason to ignore the students.

qs.q: Which detail best shows Ana's devotion to the library?
choices: Three hundred people came to the meeting.
The council voted to keep it open.
She had read every book in the animal section twice and had visited since she was five.
qs.why: Reading every animal book twice and treating the library as a second home show lasting loyalty.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Steady, respectful effort can protect something important.
Libraries are best for animal books.
qs.why: Ana's calm campaign and speech, not rule-breaking, save the library.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for talking about courage, loyalty, and fairness, and use them to read a story about a student who campaigns to save a library. They write about an injustice and a campaign, and they discuss when to defy a rule and when to work within it.

notes.va.defy.v: An open refusal to obey. Distinguish from 'disobey quietly'. The Rosa Parks example is real: keep discussion to the fact that she refused to give up her seat under a segregation law. Ask: who decides whether a law is fair?
notes.va.valiant.adj: Courage shown against real difficulty. A valiant effort can still lose. Connect to brave, courageous, heroic on a spectrum.
notes.va.dignity.n: Respect deserved by all and the calm pride in yourself. Avoid linking dignity to wealth or looks. Ask students to name one way to protect another person's dignity.
notes.va.conviction.n: A strong belief, with a second legal sense (guilty decision). Teach this sense in the senses entry and ask students to choose the sense from context.
notes.va.devotion.n: Lasting loyalty. Contrast with a quick burst of effort. Connect to devote and devoted.
notes.va.noble.adj: High moral character; not only rank. The second sense (a person of high rank) appears in old stories, so students should check context.
notes.va.rebel.n: A noun here. Rebel is neutral until we ask who and why; ask students to judge the cause, not only the act.
notes.va.injustice.n: Unfairness: in- (not) + justice. Use school-level examples first (a rule applied to only some students), then history.
notes.va.vow.v: A serious promise about the future; not a statement of fact. Practice with 'I vow to ___' sentences and discuss what makes it serious.
notes.va.campaign.n: A planned effort over time. Second sense is a verb (to campaign). Plan a mock campaign with three actions.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Ana feels the closing of the library is unfair, so injustice fits. She makes posters and collects signatures over days, which is a campaign. Theo wants to defy the council by sleeping inside, but Ana wants to speak up within the rules. I can say both want change, but they choose different ways.'
discuss: Is it ever noble to break a rule? What would make it noble?
How can a person show conviction without being rude?
misconceptions: Defy always means do something bad.
A rebel is always the hero.
Dignity belongs only to important people.
A vow and a wish are the same.
extend: Read a short biography of a person who campaigned against an injustice and list three of this unit's words that fit the person.
Plan a class campaign for a school improvement: name the injustice or problem, the goal, and three actions.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Two days later, have students sort the ten words into 'actions', 'people', and 'values'. Return to assertive, daring, and debate from earlier units when students discuss how to speak up, and reuse defy, injustice, and campaign in unit 10 on voting and government.
